"𝐖𝐞 𝐦𝐚𝐲 𝐧𝐨𝐭 𝐛𝐞 𝐟𝐢𝐫𝐢𝐧𝐠, 𝐛𝐮𝐭 𝐰𝐞'𝐫𝐞 𝐧𝐨𝐭 𝐡𝐢𝐫𝐢𝐧𝐠."
That one line from Anthropic's new "Working with AI" report sums up what I've been sensing for months.

AI's impact on jobs isn't showing up as a big layoff headline. It's showing up as a job posting that never gets written. A retirement that doesn't get backfilled. A contract that quietly doesn't renew.

Silent changes are the hardest to see, and the hardest to plan for.

𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝗺𝗲𝗮𝗻𝘀 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗷𝗼𝗯 𝘀𝗲𝗲𝗸𝗲𝗿𝘀
🔹If your applications feel like they're going into a void, it may not be you. Fewer openings means more competition for each one.
🔹Showing you can work alongside AI is becoming the baseline, not a bonus.
🔹Watch where hiring is growing, not just where it's shrinking.

𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝗺𝗲𝗮𝗻𝘀 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝘂𝘀 𝗶𝗻 𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗰𝗲
🔹 Layoff numbers won't capture this. Openings and time-to-hire will.
🔹 Build AI skills into career services now, before the pipeline narrows further.
🔹 Ask employers how they're restructuring work, not just who they're hiring.

💡 The study is small and qualitative, so treat it as an early signal, not a verdict. But early signals are worth watching.

Are you seeing this where you work? Fewer postings, more "do more with what we have"?

Stay curious. Stay current.

AI is not a software license. It is a utility bill. 📊

(And 83% of finance leaders just watched it blow past their forecast.)

For decades, enterprise software budgeting was simple:
Count the seats, negotiate an annual discount, and lock in the line item.

Generative AI broke that model.

Pigment surveyed 2,000 CFOs and finance leaders across the US and Europe. The takeaway is clear:
AI has become a cost line that corporate finance cannot reliably forecast.

The reality on the ground:

→ 83% say consumption-based AI costs pushed spending above plan
→ The typical overrun is 11% to 35%, with the average sitting at ~27%
→ 38% are more than 25% over budget, and 17% exceeded budget by over 50%
→ 40% cite unpredictable usage as their single hardest cost forecasting hurdle

Software licenses have fixed prices.
Token usage scales every time an employee prompts or an agent loops.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗺𝘆𝘁𝗵:

"Our annual IT budget will keep AI spend contained."

No. An annual budget set in October cannot predict token consumption that fluctuates every Tuesday.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝘀𝗲𝗻𝗶𝗼𝗿𝗶𝘁𝘆 𝗴𝗮𝗽:

There is a stark disconnect inside executive suites.

63% of VPs and CFOs rate their confidence in AI ROI at 9 or 10 out of 10.
Only 41% of managers agree.
In fact, managers are 3x more likely to rate actual value at 6 or below.

The leaders approving the checks feel confident.
The teams doing the operational work see the hidden drag.

𝗪𝗵𝗲𝗻 𝘂𝘀𝗮𝗴𝗲 𝗶𝘀 𝘂𝗻𝗺𝗲𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗲𝗱, 𝘁𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗴𝘀 𝗯𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗸:

𝟭. 𝗢𝘃𝗲𝗿𝗿𝘂𝗻𝘀 𝗰𝗮𝗻𝗻𝗶𝗯𝗮𝗹𝗶𝘇𝗲 𝗻𝗲𝘅𝘁 𝘆𝗲𝗮𝗿'𝘀 𝗴𝗿𝗼𝘄𝘁𝗵 🧾
→ Next year's planned budget increases slowed to 15.6%
→ This year's average 27% overrun will consume the entire increase before new projects launch

𝟮. 𝗥𝗲𝗽𝗼𝗿𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗹𝗼𝗮𝗱 𝗶𝗻𝗰𝗿𝗲𝗮𝘀𝗲𝘀 𝗶𝗻𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗮𝗱 𝗼𝗳 𝘀𝗵𝗿𝗶𝗻𝗸𝗶𝗻𝗴 🏦
→ Mature AI firms spend over 40 hours a month on executive reporting vs. 17 hours for early-stage peers
→ AI generates massive amounts of data that humans still have to reconcile and explain

𝟯. 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝘁𝗮𝗹𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗽𝗶𝗽𝗲𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗲 𝗱𝗿𝗶𝗲𝘀 𝘂𝗽
→ 33% cut entry-level hiring for roles AI can cover, but under 25% increased training
→ Cutting entry-level talent without upskilling creates a critical leadership vacuum in three years

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗹 𝗴𝗮𝗽:
Managing metered AI with static annual budgets is an operational mismatch.

FP&A needs to evolve:
Enforce rolling monthly consumption caps, mandate internal chargebacks, and establish dedicated AI cost centers with named owners.

If your finance team treats AI like a traditional software contract, you do not have budget control.

You have an open corporate card tied to an uncapped compute meter.

Does your company budget AI as a fixed license, or track it as a metered utility? 👇

P.S. Signing a software contract is predictable. Managing metered usage is capital discipline. ❤️

Sources: Pigment CFO Index Q3 2026

2 out of 58.
That's how many companies told Anthropic's own researchers that AI actually cost someone their job.
Anthropic's economics team interviewed 58 US companies using Claude, and published the results on Monday. Two-thirds said AI slowed their hiring. But only two said a role was fully eliminated.
The cuts that did happen landed on contractors. Nine firms cut contracted developers, customer support reps, and legal help — work that was already mostly offshored.
And ten firms said AI made them hire more. Implementation roles. IT support. People to make the AI actually work inside the business.
Six AI-native startups in the study said they'd need four times as many employees without AI.
So the story isn't mass layoffs. It's a freeze. Companies aren't firing people for AI — they're just not opening the role in the first place. And the first contracts to go are the ones where the work is repeatable enough for an agent to do it.
That matches what the Randstad report said two days ago: 73% of Indian employers now fill AI skill gaps with flexible talent, not permanent hires.
The work that survives is the work that needs judgment. Payroll, compliance, the decisions nobody wants an agent making alone. That's what I'm building, and it's what I'm betting on.

⬛ In today’s economy, chasing fast growth at any cost is a quick way to run out of cash.⬛

With rising costs, cautious buyers, and expensive loans across the UK, Europe, and the US, healthy growth comes down to one rule: every sale must bring real cash into your bank account, not trap your money in unpaid bills.

Here is a simple guide to growing your business safely right now

𝟭. 𝗦𝘁𝗮𝘆 𝗼𝗻 𝗧𝗼𝗽 𝗼𝗳 𝗬𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗖𝗮𝘀𝗵 𝗙𝗹𝗼𝘄
→ Keep a weekly 13 week cash forecast so you can spot money gaps months before they happen.
→ Cut unused overheads or spare stock, and ask your suppliers for more time to pay your bills.
→ Move tax money into a separate savings account as soon as you get paid so you are never caught short.
→ Test new ideas with small, low cost trials before spending big money.

𝟮. 𝗖𝗵𝗲𝗰𝗸 𝗖𝗿𝗲𝗱𝗶𝘁 𝗕𝗲𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝗬𝗼𝘂 𝗦𝗲𝗹𝗹
→ Run credit checks on new business clients before letting them pay you later.
→ Start new customers with small spending limits, or ask for a 30% to 50% deposit up front.
→ Consider credit insurance if your business relies heavily on just a few big clients.

𝟯. 𝗚𝗲𝘁 𝗣𝗮𝗶𝗱 𝗙𝗮𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗿
→ Send invoices the very day you finish the work, and set up automatic payment reminders.
→ Pay sales bonuses only when the customer actually pays the bill, not just when they sign a contract.
→ Charge late fees on overdue bills by using local laws in the UK and Europe, or clear contract rules in the US.

𝟰. 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝘁𝗲𝗰𝘁 𝗬𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗳𝗶𝘁 𝗠𝗮𝗿𝗴𝗶𝗻𝘀
→ Review your prices every three months so rising energy, wage, and supply costs do not eat your profits.
→ Focus on your most profitable services and regular monthly retainers instead of chasing low profit sales.

𝟱. 𝗚𝗿𝗼𝘄 𝗦𝗺𝗮𝗿𝘁𝗹𝘆 𝗪𝗶𝘁𝗵 𝗧𝗲𝗰𝗵 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗟𝗼𝘆𝗮𝗹 𝗖𝗹𝗶𝗲𝗻𝘁𝘀
→ Use simple automation and AI tools for admin, bookkeeping, and chasing invoices so you can handle more work without hiring too fast.
→ Look after your best existing customers with great service and extra offers, since keeping them is much cheaper than finding new ones.
Remember, a sale is not real until the money is in your bank.

Which of these steps is your biggest focus right now?

"Where should we start with AI?"

Most companies answer this with the most impressive idea in the room. A customer-facing chatbot. An agent that runs sales. Then it stalls for months.

The first AI projects that actually pay off tend to look boring:

Good first project: pulling fields from invoices, orders or forms into your system
Risky first project: an AI that talks to customers on its own

Good first project: drafting replies that a person reviews and sends
Risky first project: replies that go out with nobody checking

Good first project: sorting and tagging incoming emails or support tickets
Risky first project: "automate the whole support team"

Good first project: summarizing long calls, documents or reports for the team
Risky first project: decisions about money, contracts or hiring

A quick test before you pick one:
• It happens many times a week
• A mistake is cheap and easy to spot
• Someone on the team can tell you what "good" looks like
• You can measure the time it saves

Small wins build trust. Trust is what lets you take on the bigger ideas later.

No Layoffs. No Hiring. Just Fewer Marketing Jobs.

Marketing jobs are disappearing. But the strange part - Nobody is announcing layoffs. They're just not replacing people who leave.

A content writer resigns. The company doesn't hire another one.
A designer leaves. AI takes over part of the work.
A junior marketer's contract ends. The remaining team manages somehow. And slowly, the team becomes smaller. This is already happening.

A survey of 100 B2B marketing leaders by Wynter found that 47% of companies had reduced, eliminated or stopped backfilling marketing roles because of AI. Only 7% reported visible team shrinkage. The rest happened quietly.

Look at Klarna.
Its employee count fell from 5,527 in 2022 to 2,831 by the end of 2025.
That's almost half the workforce. The company has openly credited AI and operational efficiency for this transformation, with much of the reduction happening through natural attrition rather than layoffs.

But here's the part I find more interesting.
Gartner surveyed 1,303 senior leaders in 2026.
18% of marketing leaders had already eliminated certain roles due to automation.
16% had created new roles. And Gartner predicts that by 2030, most high-performing marketing teams could eliminate traditional entry-level positions.

Now, think about the consequences.
Today, a company saves money by not hiring a junior content writer, designer or marketing executive.
Fair enough. The numbers may look better.
But who trains the next generation of marketing managers?
Who learns campaign execution before becoming a campaign strategist?
Who makes mistakes, understands customers and develops business judgment?

You cannot hire a team full of experienced marketers in 2032 if nobody gets the opportunity to become one today.

This is the challenge CEOs and CMOs need to think about.

AI can reduce the number of people needed to execute work. But companies still need people who understand customers, make decisions and own business results. The real question isn't how many employees AI can replace.

It's whether companies are building the next generation of leaders while making that transition.

Are companies becoming more efficient today at the cost of their talent pipeline tomorrow?

🌍 KSA → UAE → Europe: Where Should Your Career Go Next?

For many engineers and skilled professionals working in the Gulf, one question eventually comes up:

Should I build my career in Saudi Arabia, move to the UAE, or target Europe?

There is no single correct answer. Each region offers a different combination of career growth, income, lifestyle, education, technology and long-term opportunities.

🇸🇦 Saudi Arabia — Build Experience & Take Part in a Fast-Changing Market

Key cities: Riyadh, Jeddah, Dammam, NEOM/Tabuk, AlUla

Saudi Arabia is undergoing major economic diversification through Vision 2030, with investment in infrastructure, technology, logistics, tourism, healthcare, energy and new industries.

For engineers, this can mean exposure to large-scale projects, FM/O&M, MEP, HVAC, energy, manufacturing, construction and emerging technologies.

Vision 2030 also identifies human-capital development, lifelong learning, vocational training, technology localization and attracting global talent as priorities.

Best strategy:
Build strong technical experience + certifications + project exposure + professional network.

---

🇦🇪 UAE — International Business & Career Networking

Key cities: Dubai, Abu Dhabi, Sharjah, Ras Al Khaimah

The UAE offers a highly international business environment with opportunities across construction, facilities management, engineering, technology, aviation, logistics, energy, finance and real estate.

The UAE government provides dedicated job-search, training and employment services, while its official employment system requires appropriate work authorization rather than working on a visit/tourist visa.

Best strategy:
Build a strong GCC CV → develop specialized skills → network with recruiters and hiring managers → target MNCs and specialized engineering roles.

---

🇪🇺 Europe — Long-Term Professional & Educational Development

Key cities/hubs:
🇩🇪 Munich, Frankfurt, Berlin, Stuttgart
🇳🇱 Amsterdam, Eindhoven, Rotterdam
🇫🇷 Paris, Lyon
🇮🇪 Dublin
🇸🇪 Stockholm, Gothenburg
🇩🇰 Copenhagen
🇦🇹 Vienna
🇵🇱 Warsaw, Kraków

Europe is not one job market. Every country has different immigration, salary, tax, language and employment requirements.

However, EU data show that job quality has improved over the past decade, particularly in areas such as earnings, job security and working time. The EU employment rate reached 76.1% in 2025.

For highly qualified non-EU professionals, the EU Blue Card can provide a route to live and work in participating EU countries when the relevant qualification/skill, employment contract and salary requirements are met.

In 2024, EU countries issued approximately 78,100 Blue Cards, with Germany issuing about 72% of them.

🎓 Study vs. Work

If your objective is education + research + long-term professional development, Europe can be attractive.

If your objective is rapid project exposure + GCC experience + international networking, KSA and UAE can be strong stepping stones.

The important question is not:

❌ “Which region is best?”

It is:

✅ “Which region is best for my current career stage?”

---

🏥 Life & Health

Quality of life cannot be judged only by salary.

Consider:

• Healthcare access
• Working hours
• Annual leave
• Housing costs
• Transportation
• Climate
• Family environment
• Education for children
• Social security
• Taxes
• Long-term residency
• Work-life balance

Europe generally has stronger institutional social-protection systems, but taxation and living costs vary significantly by country.

The Gulf can provide attractive professional and financial opportunities, but housing, healthcare, schooling and other costs must be considered individually.

Net income + expenses + benefits = the real financial picture.

---

💻 Technology & Future Skills

Wherever you live, the winning strategy is increasingly the same:

Technical expertise + Digital skills + AI + Communication + Project Management

For an HVAC/Mechanical Engineer, for example:

HVAC/Chillers → Controls/BMS → Data & Analytics → AI → Energy Efficiency → Project Management

The engineer who understands both physical systems and digital technology will be better positioned for the future.

---

🇸🇦➡️🇪🇺 If You Are Working in KSA and Want to Move to Europe

Don't think:

“I need to leave Saudi Arabia immediately.”

Think:

“How can I use my Gulf experience to become a stronger European candidate?”

A practical pathway can be:

KSA Experience
↓
Specialized Technical Skills
↓
Certifications & Projects
↓
Strong CV + LinkedIn
↓
European Job Market Research
↓
Targeted Applications & Networking
↓
Employer Offer / Appropriate Visa Route
↓
🇪🇺 Move to Europe

For highly qualified professionals, investigate the specific country's work-permit routes and, where applicable, the EU Blue Card. Requirements differ between countries.

🚀 My Perspective

KSA can be a platform for experience.
UAE can be a platform for international business and networking.
Europe can be a platform for long-term professional, educational and social development.

But none of these regions automatically guarantees success.

Your skills, experience, language ability, qualifications, network and ability to adapt will ultimately determine how far you can go.

Don't just chase a country. Build a career profile that gives you the freedom to choose the country.

Organisations often treat AI as a technology project. I have mapped what I think it really takes to deliver AI at scale. Here are 35 capabilities across seven domains:
🛡️ Governance, risk and compliance: AI policy and AI Councils, ISO/IEC 42001, the EU AI Act, POPIA, vendor contracts and Responsible AI
📊 Data: data governance, quality, engineering, metadata and ontology, and data protection
💻 Build and engineering: coding, prompt and context engineering, agent and API design (MCP, Copilot Studio), and DevSecOps/MLOps
💡 Designing solutions: solution architecture, choosing the right model for each task, process automation and UI/UX
🔧 Run and operate: platform management, monitoring, observability, cyber security (OWASP LLM Top 10, MITRE ATLAS) and resilience
🤝 People and support: helpdesk, AI literacy training, change management, communities of practice, and audit and assurance
💰 Delivery and finance: project and portfolio management, AI FinOps, and business cases built on measurable value
The key point is that most of these capabilities already exist in your organisation: ✅ 9 need a sharper focus from existing roles 📚 18 need additional training for existing roles 🆕 8 are new roles, such as prompt and context engineering, model selection, agent design, Responsible AI and an AI community of practice
Being ready for AI is mainly about building skills, not hiring. Start by finding out where your people already are, explore, train and scale.

Last week I wrote that most procurement problems start when nobody pins down what we're buying.
 
Here's what happens next.
 
You pin it down. You run a clean sourcing. You sign a good deal.
 
Then, six weeks into the project, someone says: "Can we also connect this to Coupa?"
 
Go-live hasn't moved. Security has a new question. And the supplier replies with a change request and a price tag.
 
Suddenly nobody is talking about the project anymore. They're talking about whose fault it is.
 
In 8 years of IT procurement, I've seen a late integration request turn a smooth rollout into weeks of back-and-forth. I'm convinced this is the most expensive problem in our field, even though it never shows up on the quote.
 
The fix isn't tougher negotiation. It's simple, a bit unglamorous and it works:
 
→ Agree how change will be handled before it happens. Who approves, how it's priced, how fast we respond. Then a change is just a step, not a fight.
 
→ Tell the supplier early. Share what you know and what you don't. Early news gets you flexibility. Late news gets you a defensive supplier.
 
→ Ask "do we truly need this?" before saying yes. Put business, IT and security in one room. A big chunk of late requests turns out to be nice to have.
 
→ Let AI do the repetitive work. Comparing contract versions, checking clauses against standard terms, spotting gaps. That frees your time for the conversations that need a human.
 
→ Value the supplier who warns you early. A single "this will break" at the right time saves more than a price cut.

Your chatbot is not an AI agent. 
And most small businesses are about 
to pay agent prices for a workflow.

Agentic AI is software that takes a goal, works out the steps, and acts inside the tools you already use.
 
A chatbot waits for a question.
A fixed automation repeats the same path every time.
An agent decides the next step when the facts change.
 
That gap is the whole purchase decision.
 
Gartner has warned that over 40% of agentic AI projects will be canceled by the end of 2027. Not because the idea is fake. Because the job was too wide, the bill grew, and nobody wrote a rule for when to turn it off.
 
What actually earns its keep for a small firm is narrow:
• An overdue invoice, with the real facts in the follow-up
• A new inquiry that lands at 11 pm
• A support ticket sorted before a person ever opens it
 
The test is smaller than the sales page. One job. One page of rules. Thirty days. Keep it only if the numbers you wrote down on day one actually moved.
 
The guide also prices the tools many teams already pay for, and names the jobs an agent should prepare but never send: refunds, contracts, and hiring decisions.

For founders writing a 2027 hiring plan, start with AT&T in 1969. --- 𝐀𝐛𝐨𝐮𝐭 𝟏,𝟎𝟎𝟎,𝟎𝟎𝟎 𝐞𝐦𝐩𝐥𝐨𝐲𝐞𝐞𝐬, worth $245.6B in 2026 dollars. 

Anthropic went public last week with 𝟓,𝟑𝟎𝟎 𝐞𝐦𝐩𝐥𝐨𝐲𝐞𝐞𝐬 and a $1.17T market cap.  

The table comes from Ben Thompson's Stratechery piece this morning, "The Individual Exception." He takes the most valuable company of each decade and adjusts everything for inflation except headcount.  

GE in 1999 had 340,000 people and a $1.03T market cap. Apple today has 167,000 and $5.07T. 

NVIDIA has 42,000 and $3.99T, which Thompson puts at $95M of market cap per employee. His chart only works on a log scale.  I ran his numbers per person. AT&T in 1969 comes out around $246K of market value per employee. Anthropic is about $221M. 

𝐑𝐨𝐮𝐠𝐡𝐥𝐲 𝟗𝟎𝟎𝐱 𝐢𝐧 𝟓𝟕 𝐲𝐞𝐚𝐫𝐬.  Thompson opens with his own week. Since Thursday he has built a remote-control system for his entire studio and an agent harness that farms work out to the computers in his house. A few years ago that would have taken teams weeks or months. His refrain is "It only takes an individual."  The title is about Jensen Huang. 

Nvidia's board accepted his resignation on November 12 and said a week later it would not bring him back. On November 23 it reinstated him, unanimously. Thompson points out Huang built Nvidia as a vehicle for one person, himself.  From Taipei the table reads a little differently. Nvidia can run on 42,000 people partly because its chips are made by TSMC and its servers are assembled by contract manufacturers like Foxconn. 

TSMC alone has more than 80,000 employees, and its 2024 annual report counts 24,404 technicians. Foxconn employs hundreds of thousands. A lot of the headcount sits further down the supply chain, much of it with Taiwanese companies.  AI is shrinking the design side first. Thompson's week shows it. 

𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐟𝐚𝐛 𝐟𝐥𝐨𝐨𝐫 𝐢𝐬 𝐰𝐡𝐞𝐫𝐞 𝐈 𝐞𝐱𝐩𝐞𝐜𝐭 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐧𝐞𝐱𝐭 𝐡𝐞𝐚𝐝𝐜𝐨𝐮𝐧𝐭 𝐜𝐮𝐫𝐯𝐞 𝐭𝐨 𝐛𝐞𝐧𝐝, through robotics.  My bet is that the next company to beat Anthropic on market value per employee designs in California and builds through Taiwan, on fab floors with more robots than technicians.

Two-thirds of the companies Anthropic  interviewed for its new Working with AI report are hiring less because of AI. Only two of the 58 saw AI automation fully eliminate a role. That gap is the number I'd put in front of every CIO finishing a 2027 AOP this month.

The cuts are showing up as requisitions that never get opened and contracts that don't renew. Nine companies told Anthropic they cut contracted developers, customer service, legal and back-office work, much of it already offshore. One finance company let go of well over 100 offshore data and developer contractors.

I run solutions and strategy at BayOne Solutions with delivery teams in India, LATAM, and the Philippines, so I read that section twice. I think the buyers are right. Modular work handed off with low quality expectations was always going to be the first thing an agent absorbs. Any provider still pricing that work by the hour should expect to lose the line in your 2027 budget.

The part I'd push CIOs to act on sits further down. The highest-value applications in the study required reorganizing roles and process. The bottlenecks were internal: reviewing AI output, uneven adoption, downstream teams that couldn't keep pace with faster coding. Customer skepticism and regulation barely came up.

Where I'd move money in the 2027 plan:

1. Fund the review layer before you fund more generation. Code review, QA and approvals are where AI output piles up.
2. Keep vertical point-solution contracts short. One interviewee said a purchased system would be obsolete in three months.
3. Put real dollars into consolidating data that agents and nontechnical staff can query, with guardrails for people shipping their own apps.
4. Line-item role redesign and redeployment. A law firm in the study paired junior associates with senior attorneys to mark up AI first drafts. It kept its people and got the value.
5. Reprice offshore and contractor spend against outcomes, with agents doing the modular tasks and humans owning the exceptions.

An engineering leader at a health management company told the researchers they added capacity by buying tokens instead of hiring people. If your AOP books tokens under IT opex and headcount under the business units, nobody in the room will see that trade being made.

Working in finance in an SME means getting involved in a bit of everything. Cash flow, tax, reporting, budgets, systems, commercial decisions … often with something unexpected thrown in.

It’s a privilege to get that exposure. I’ve been lucky to develop the skills to think across finance and understand how the different parts fit together.

Starting Financial AI Studios has meant getting involved in a much wider range of things, several of which are clearly outside my skill set.

I’ve had to think about:

* Branding and website design (yes even having an opinion on fonts!!)
* Marketing - explaining what we do clearly and deciding how to reach people.
* Sales - pricing, proposals, finding opportunities and following up.
* Legal matters - contracts, liability and ownership of the work we create.
* Policies - how we handle data and use AI responsibly.
* Hiring - what help we need, what we can afford and how to support someone joining.
* Keeping things running - suppliers, insurance, IT and what happens if something stops working.

I can assess the financial implications of those decisions. That doesn’t mean I know how to design a website or run a marketing campaign.

There’s a lot to learn, and part of it is knowing when to ask for help. Another part is accepting that something can be good enough for now when there are other things that need attention.

For anyone who’s made the move from employment to running a business - what did you find yourself getting involved in that you’d never expected?
